items.title: 14.2.8 Work done By a Constant Force

blocks.text: If a constant force \(\underline{F}\), applied to a body, acts at an angle \(\theta\) to the direction of motion, then the work done by \(\underline{F}\) is defined to be the product of the component of \(\underline{F}\) in the direction of the displacement and the distance that the body moves.
In figure, a constant force \(\underline{F}\) acting on a body, displaces it from \(A\) to \(B\).

blocks.alt: A grey block on rough ground at A is pulled by a force F at angle theta above the horizontal. A dashed vertical line drops from the tip of F to the horizontal arrow, with a right-angle mark. Inside the ground a hollow double arrow marks the part labelled magnitude of F cos theta. A dashed outline shows the block at B, and the distance d from A to B is marked below.
blocks.caption: Figure: a constant force F at angle θ to the motion moves a body from A to B (original drawing after the textbook's figure)

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why only the component? The part of the force across the motion (the vertical part \(|\underline{F}|\sin\theta\) in the figure) does not help to move the body forward, so it does no work. Only \(|\underline{F}|\cos\theta\), the projection of \(\underline{F}\) on the displacement, counts. Multiplying it by the distance \(|\underline{d}|\) gives
\[W = |\underline{F}||\underline{d}|\cos\theta = \underline{F} \cdot \underline{d}\]
So work is a dot product. Special cases: \(\theta = 0\) gives \(W = |\underline{F}||\underline{d}|\) (largest); \(\theta = 90^{\circ}\) gives \(W = 0\); an obtuse \(\theta\) gives negative work (the force opposes the motion).
Example of ours: \(\underline{F} = 3\underline{i} + 4\underline{j}\) newtons moves a body through \(\underline{d} = 5\underline{i}\) metres: \(W = 15 + 0 = 15\) joules (Nm).

blocks.title: Example 14
blocks.problem: The constant forces \(2\underline{i} + 5\underline{j} + 6\underline{k}\) and \(-\underline{i} - 2\underline{j} - \underline{k}\) acting on a body, displaced form position \(P(4, -3, -2)\) to \(Q(6, 1, -3)\). Find the total work done.
steps:
Given: forces \(\underline{F}_{1} = 2\underline{i} + 5\underline{j} + 6\underline{k}\), \(\underline{F}_{2} = -\underline{i} - 2\underline{j} - \underline{k}\); the body moves from \(P(4, -3, -2)\) to \(Q(6, 1, -3)\).
To find: the total work done.
Method: add the forces to get the total (resultant) force \(\underline{F}\), find the displacement \(\underline{d} = \overrightarrow{PQ}\), then \(W = \underline{F} \cdot \underline{d}\).

Step 1: Total force
\[\underline{F} = (2\underline{i} + 5\underline{j} + 6\underline{k}) + (-\underline{i} - 2\underline{j} - \underline{k})\]
\[= \underline{i} + 3\underline{j} + 5\underline{k}\]
Why: forces acting together add as vectors, component by component.

Step 2: Displacement
\[\underline{d} = \overrightarrow{PQ} = (6 - 4)\underline{i} + (1 + 3)\underline{j} + (-3 + 2)\underline{k}\]
\[= 2\underline{i} + 4\underline{j} - \underline{k}\]
Why: \(\overrightarrow{PQ}\) = position vector of \(Q\) minus position vector of \(P\).

Step 3: Work done
\[W = \underline{F} \cdot \underline{d} = (\underline{i} + 3\underline{j} + 5\underline{k}) \cdot (2\underline{i} + 4\underline{j} - \underline{k})\]
\[= (1)(2) + (3)(4) + (5)(-1)\]
\[= 2 + 12 - 5 = 9\]
Why: work = force dot displacement.

Check:
Work of each force separately: \(\underline{F}_{1} \cdot \underline{d} = 4 + 20 - 6 = 18\), \(\underline{F}_{2} \cdot \underline{d} = -2 - 8 + 1 = -9\); total \(18 - 9 = 9\).
blocks.answer: Total work done \(= 9\) units (the book writes \(9\) Nm, taking forces in newtons and distances in metres).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book prints "displaced form position"; it should be "displaced from position".

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. Work done by a constant force: \(W = \underline{F} \cdot \underline{d} = |\underline{F}||\underline{d}|\cos\theta\).
2. Several forces: add them first (or add their separate works); the answer is the same.
3. Displacement \(= \overrightarrow{PQ}\) = (final point) \(-\) (initial point).
4. Work is a scalar; with forces in newtons and distances in metres its unit is Nm (joule).

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Taking \(\overrightarrow{PQ}\) as \(P - Q\); the displacement is final minus initial.
2. Using the position vector of \(Q\) instead of the displacement \(\overrightarrow{PQ}\).
3. Writing work as a vector; work is a number.
